Your statement is false and it shows your ignorance regarding both the intent of the Affordable Care Act and how health care systems actually work.

The Affordable Care Act was meant to make health insurance affordable relative to income. That is why it uses income based premium caps, tax credits, out of pocket limits, and consumer protections. Before the ACA, insurers could deny coverage, impose lifetime caps, and price people out simply for being sick. After the ACA, people could actually buy and keep insurance without facing medical bankruptcy. That was the law’s purpose and it succeeded by every measurable coverage metric.

The ACA is not single payer health care. It relies almost entirely on private insurance companies. Insurers still set premiums, manage provider networks, process claims, and compete for customers. The government does not act as the universal insurer and does not replace private coverage. Calling the ACA single payer is simply incorrect.

Single payer systems themselves are also not some unworkable theory. Versions of single payer or near single payer health care operate successfully all over the world. Countries like Canada, the United Kingdom, France, Australia, Japan, and others provide universal coverage, lower per capita health care costs, and equal or better health outcomes than the United States. Whether someone prefers that model or not is a policy debate, but claiming it does not work is contradicted by decades of real world evidence.

Rising health care costs were not designed by Congressional Democrats or President Obama. Costs were rising rapidly for decades before the ACA due to hospital consolidation, drug pricing, fee for service incentives, and provider market power. The ACA did not create those costs. It reduced uncompensated care, slowed spending growth compared to prior trends, and shifted costs away from families who previously absorbed them directly.

If Democrats had designed rising costs, repealing or weakening the ACA would lower prices. It does not. Removing subsidies raises premiums for consumers. Weakening coverage rules increases medical debt. Eliminating protections does nothing to control hospital or drug company pricing. Every serious analysis shows repeal makes affordability worse, not better.

The ACA was designed to expand coverage, protect people from financial ruin, and stabilize insurance markets. Rising costs are a broader American health system problem. Blaming the ACA or pretending it is single payer is misinformation, not analysis.
